Hi Nina, Thanks for reaching out. Happy to help with this.

I usually charge on an hourly basis for model reviews $10/hour. The reason I don't do a flat fee is that with financial models, you can't really just "spot check" one section and call it done. Even a single wrong input or formula tends to ripple through the whole model, so a proper review means going through it end to end and tightening up whatever needs it along the way.

On your model specifically, I'd be looking closely at the data you've fed in versus your source documents, checking that the formulas and links are working the way they should across sheets, and going through the key assumptions to see if they're reasonable and well supported. I'd also want to check the valuation side properly WACC, cost of equity, Beta, and how they've been applied plus the tax treatment, since that's an area where small errors often go unnoticed until they affect the output.

Once you share the template and data, I can take a quick look and give you a rough sense of how many hours it'll likely take, so you have a clear idea of cost before we start.

Let me know if that works for you, and feel free to send the files over whenever ready.

Best,
Muhammad Abdullah

Please confirm on the following points : 
1. Site list conflict
Your Demand Analysis report and your Business Case use two different 8-site networks (Demand Analysis includes Bowden-Lacombe, Wetaskiwin-Ponoka, Bassano, and Atmore & the Business Case includes Red Deer, Fort McMurray-Suncor, and Medicine Hat instead). Which site list should we treat as final for the financial model the Business Case list, since it has the capital allocation figures?

2. Opex figure conflict
Your original brief states steady-state operating costs of CAD 30-40M/year for the 8-site network, but the Business Case Appendix 1 states annual O&M of only CAD 2.8-3.9M/year a roughly 9x difference. Can you confirm which figure (or cost basis) should be used for the financial model's operating cost assumption?

3. Availability payment sizing target
Should the availability payment be sized only to reach a target minimum DSCR (currently 1.35x), or should it also be sized to deliver a minimum equity IRR (the Business Case cites a 12-18% target range for infrastructure equity)? Under the current DSCR-only approach, equity IRR still comes out negative even after adding the availability payment.

4. Programwide/shared costs
The Business Case's $155M Reference Case includes $11.6M for programwide shared costs (digital platform, program management) plus a $9M reserve/9th-site allowance, on top of the $134.5M in site-level capex. Should we add these as separate line items in the model, or are they excluded from the 8-site financial model scope?

5. Financing terms confirmation
The Business Case describes senior debt at 60-75% of capital, priced at 200-300bps over Government of Canada bond yields, plus optional mezzanine debt. We've modeled a simplified 70/30 debt/equity split at 6% flat. Do you want us to reflect the mezzanine layer separately, or is the simplified single-tranche structure acceptable for this stage?

6. Tax/depreciation
We've applied a flat 25% tax on EBITDA with no depreciation shield modeled yet. Is that acceptable for this stage, or do you need depreciation/CCA (Capital Cost Allowance) reflected given this is a real submission to government?

messages.text:
Hi Nuna,

Sure I will make the required changes. The model looks detailed because it's built on individual drivers each revenue stream (parking, pods, fleet, digital, ancillary) and each cost line is calculated separately from its own assumption, rather than typed in as one lump number. I did it this way on purpose so that when the government reviewer asks "where does this figure come from?", every number traces back to a source on the Assumptions tab. That's what makes it defensible.

The trade-off is exactly what you're feeling , more drivers , more rows to look at. I can go either way, so I'd rather you decide:

(a) Keep it driver-based (defensible, more rows), or
(b) Collapse it to a summary model a handful of top-level lines (total revenue, total cost, debt, availability payment, returns) with the detailed build moved to hidden/backing tabs. The front page becomes very short and clean; the detail is still there if anyone wants to open it.

I can make it a one-pager but still has the audit trail underneath. Tell me which you'd prefer and I'll restructure accordingly.

A few structuring options came up that could genuinely strengthen your pitch to government. These aren't in the model yet; I'm flagging them because any one of them could be the thing that makes the submission stand out. Such as:

1\. Government-funds-first, then sublet against the income ("build-then-transfer"). The Province funds or co-funds the capex up front (cheapest capital in the room), then leases/sublets the operating network to a private operator who pays a concession fee back against parking, pod and fleet income. This flips the story instead of government paying an availability payment out, government recovers a return in. I can model this as a third case (Case C) it may show a far lower net cost to the Province than the availability-payment route.

2\. Availability payment now, tapering to a revenue-share later. Rather than a flat 30-year payment, structure it so the Province pays more in the early ramp-up years (when revenue is thin) and then, once the network matures and throws off surplus cash, the Province shares in the upside clawing back part of what it paid in. Same bankability, lower lifetime net cost, and it reads as a partnership rather than a subsidy.

3\. Toll / user-levy overlay on the corridor. If these sites sit on designated freight corridors, a small per-truck corridor levy (or a portion of an existing road-use charge) could be ring-fenced to part-fund the network. That directly reduces the availability payment the government has to find from general revenue the users who benefit help pay.

4\. Phased equity exit / refinancing at stabilisation. Model the Province (or the original equity) selling down its stake to a pension fund or infrastructure fund once the network is built and de-risked (around year 5-7). De-risked, cash-yielding infrastructure sells at a premium so early capital gets recycled out at a profit and redeployed into Phase 2, instead of being locked up for 30 years.

5\. Anchor / cornerstone tenant revenue. Lock in one or two large fleets or a fuel/EV/retail partner on a long-term take-or-pay contract at the flagship hubs before financial close. Even a modest guaranteed floor on revenue materially improves the DSCR and can shrink the availability payment lenders require it's the single fastest way to make the numbers look stronger without changing the build.

Happy to build any of these into the model as additional cases options 1 and 2 in particular could meaningfully cut the headline cost to government, which is exactly what makes a submission persuasive. Let me know which direction you'd like, and whether to go simple (b) or keep it detailed, and I'll turn it around.

Best,
Muhammad
